title: Brick walls and glass ceilings
subtitle: hit the roof, a window of opportunity, behind closed doors
summary: See how English builds metaphors out of buildings - walls, ceilings, roofs, doors and keys - and use each one with the right meaning.

lesson.heading: Bricks and cement
lesson.text: Literally, **cement** fixes bricks firmly in place. Figuratively, it makes relationships solid - and it works as both a noun and a verb. Literally, a **brick wall** stops you going any further; figuratively, to **come up against a brick wall** is to meet a barrier you cannot get past. And to **build someone up** is to praise them so much that expectations of them rise.

examples.text: Let's have a drink together to **cement** our partnership.
When I tried to find out who had opened my letters, I **came up against a brick wall**.
The press has **built up** the young footballer so much that it must be extra pressure on him.

left.label: Literal
left.text: A ceiling is the surface above your head that you cannot go through.
examples: The ceiling in the old hall is beautifully painted.

right.label: Figurative
right.text: So a **ceiling** is a limit on something, and **the glass ceiling** is the invisible barrier that stops people, especially women, from rising to top positions at work - you can see through it, but you cannot get past it.
examples: They put a **ceiling** on the number of planned redundancies.
Many women still hit **the glass ceiling** in their late thirties.

lesson.heading: Roofs and floors
lesson.text: The roof is the top of a building, so when prices **go through the roof** they rise in a rapid, uncontrolled way (informal), and when someone **hits the roof** they get very angry. If **the roof falls in** on your world, your world collapses - and, in the opposite direction, **the floor gives way** when you faint.

examples.text: The cost of petrol has **gone through the roof** in the last six months.
My mother will **hit the roof** when she sees what we've done.
**The roof fell in** on my world on the day he died.

lesson.heading: Windows: an opening
lesson.text: A window is an opening, both literally and metaphorically. A **window of opportunity** is a chance to do something special, open for a limited time only. And when a quality or an idea **goes out of the window**, it departs - as though thrown out through it.

examples.text: If you see a **window of opportunity**, then take advantage of it.
Once the boys started going around together, common sense **went out of the window**.

lesson.heading: Towers: height and distance
lesson.text: A tower is very tall, so it suggests distance from ordinary people: someone who lives in an **ivory tower** does not know about the unpleasant, ordinary things of life. Height can also be strength: a person who is a **tower of strength** is extremely strong emotionally. And to **tower above** others is to be outstandingly tall - or outstanding in some other way.

examples.text: Academics are often criticised for living in their **ivory towers**.
Our friends were a **tower of strength** when our house burnt down.
Lauren **towers above** all her classmates, although she is one of the youngest.
Ben **towers over** all the other lawyers in his firm. He is by far the most able.

lesson.heading: Entrances: gateways, doors and keys
rows: give an opportunity to get somewhere
close the door on the past
be the thing that makes something possible

lesson.heading: Doors and keys in use
lesson.text: A gateway lets you into a place, so **a gateway to** something gives you the way in. A door can be opened or shut, and how you go through it matters: **by the back door** means unofficially, and **behind closed doors** means in secret. A key unlocks things, so it stands for whatever is essential or most important.

examples.text: A degree in law is **a gateway to** a well-paid job.
Failing his final exams **closed a lot of doors** for him.
Jack came into the business **by the back door** - the manager knew him from university.
The decision was taken **behind closed doors** and no one knows exactly why.
Knowing the right people is **the key to** success in that country.

lesson.heading: More building metaphors
rows: keep the wolf from the door
earn just enough to survive on
put things right close to home first

lesson.text: Hit the roof is about anger; go through the roof is about prices. Same roof, very different meanings.

exercises.prompt: Match the two halves of each building metaphor.
The price of fuel has ___ through the roof.
exercises.explanation: To go through the roof is to increase in a rapid, uncontrolled way.

exercises.prompt: Lucy's father ___ the roof when he saw that she'd dyed her hair purple.
exercises.explanation: To hit the roof is to get very angry.

exercises.prompt: We hope that this scientist's work may ___ the key to solving the problem.
exercises.explanation: Something that holds or provides the key to a problem is what makes solving it possible.

exercises.prompt: A degree in economics ___ the door to a number of interesting job opportunities.
exercises.explanation: To open doors is to create opportunities.

exercises.prompt: Whenever you try to initiate something in this company you find that, sooner or later, you ___ up against a brick wall.
exercises.explanation: To come up against a brick wall is to meet a barrier you cannot get past.

exercises.prompt: Ben ___ over all the other lawyers in his firm. He is by far the most able.
exercises.explanation: To tower above or over others is to be outstandingly tall, or outstanding in some other way.

exercises.prompt: Her argument with the board last year has, unfortunately, ___ a lot of doors for her in this company.
exercises.explanation: To close or shut doors is to remove opportunities.

exercises.prompt: The roof ___ in on their world the day that war was declared.
exercises.explanation: When the roof falls in on someone's world, their world collapses.

exercises.prompt: My brother is always enormously supportive whenever I have a problem. How would you say that?
options: He is a tower of strength.
He lives in an ivory tower.
He comes in by the back door.
exercises.explanation: A tower of strength is someone extremely strong in an emotional rather than a physical sense.

exercises.prompt: We'll never know what the two Presidents said to each other when they met in private.
exercises.explanation: Doing something behind closed doors suggests secrecy; by the back door suggests doing it unofficially.

exercises.prompt: Winning an Olympic medal can provide an opportunity to develop a career in the media.
options: can be the gateway to a career in the media
can be the glass ceiling of a career in the media
can hit the roof of a career in the media
can cement a career in the media
exercises.explanation: To be a gateway to something is to give an opportunity to get somewhere.

exercises.statement: Having children often cements a marriage - it makes the relationship more solid.
exercises.explanation: Correct - cement holds bricks firmly in place, and the metaphor works the same way for relationships.

exercises.statement: 'Lena has built Max up so much' means Lena has criticised Max heavily.
exercises.explanation: To build someone up is to praise them in a way that increases expectations of them.
